title: The fearless Formless
hookLine: Nanak says the Formless alone is fearless; all else is dust by comparison (Asa di Var, ang 464)

cards: If you've been on this path since the first year, you know the word. It sits in the Mool Mantar, the opening lines of the Guru Granth Sahib, right after the Creator and before without hate: nirbhau. Without fear.
Yesterday's salok ended on it, after a whole universe of trembling: only the Formless is without fear. Today's salok, the next one in the var, starts there and refuses to move on quickly.
Nanak, it says, the Formless is fearless. Then it looks at everything else people admire.

teach.b: Two words carry this salok on ang 464. Nirbhau: nir, without, and bhau, the fear and awe we met yesterday.
And nirankar: nir again, without, and akar, form or shape. The Formless. Together they answer a very human question: is there anything that isn't afraid?
Everything else, yesterday's salok said, lives in awe.
And anything with a form can break; it can be lost. The salok goes on to list what people admire and tell stories about, and sets each beside the Formless. So many celebrated figures are like dust.

So many tales are told and retold, so many learned arguments made. People dance and sing for a crowd. Others wear earrings and necklaces worth a fortune, and the bodies that wear them, the salok says plainly, turn to ash.

teach.h: WISDOM COMES BY GRACE, NOT TALK.
teach.b: Real wisdom isn't found through talk. Speaking of the One is as hard as iron. It comes by grace; cleverness and display only wear a person out.
Here's why it matters. So much fear attaches to forms: a body getting sick, a job disappearing, a reputation cracking, a person leaving. The salok doesn't call those fears silly.
Forms really do pass. What it offers is a place to stand.
If only the Formless is fearless, then the way through fear, in Sikh teaching, isn't to become hard and fearless yourself. It's to stay close to the One who is.
Some Sikh teachers put it in a short phrase: the one who fears the One fears nothing else.

how: Sikhs meet the word nirbhau every day in the Mool Mantar, and hear this salok on the fearless Formless when Asa di Var is sung at dawn.

o: without fear, like the Formless One
brave enough to fight any enemy
free from every worry by effort

games.q: without fear, without form — tap the pairs.
p: the bodies wearing them turn to ash

s: the word nirbhau first appears in the Asa di Var
it's already in the Mool Mantar, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib.
the salok says speaking of the One is as hard as iron
wisdom isn't found through talk; it comes by grace.
the salok calls people's fears silly
it says forms really do pass, and points to the Formless as the only one without fear.

games.q: a fear grips you about something you could lose. what does the salok point toward?
o: become hard and fearless on your own.
stay close to the Formless, the only one without fear.
hold the thing tighter so it can't break.
games.why: every form can break, the salok says, even jewels and bodies. only the Formless is fearless, and Sikh teaching places the way through fear there.

practice: Let one real fear come to mind, not the biggest, and notice the form it clings to: your health, your money, a person.
Set it beside the whole sky, the wind and rivers moving in their order, and watch it take its true size; you don't have to make it disappear. If you pray, say nirbhau, nirankar, quietly.

wordCard.voice: Nirbhau, without fear: nir, without, and bhau, the fear and awe met yesterday, the word the Mool Mantar gives right after without hate.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: without fear, without form; nir- means without in both words.

carryVoice: Your line: only he is fearless. Forms pass; the Formless doesn't. Five hundred forty-four days now.

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok M1 (Nanak nirbhau nirankar), Ang 464–465
